posts.text:
Most apartment posts show the pool.
Renters are also choosing the neighborhood.

The coffee shop on the corner, the Saturday market, the park where the dogs meet up. Those are part of what a renter is signing up for, and they rarely show up in a listing.

A few neighborhood posts a month can answer questions a floor plan can't: What is it like to walk outside on a Sunday? Where do people actually go?

The rule we use: only post places that are real, open and close by, and check them before they go out.

What's one local spot your residents mention most?

posts.alt: Navy card with the headline Renters don't read your brochure. They ask a question.
posts.text:
Renters don't read your brochure.
They ask a question, and they expect a straight answer.

Can I bring two dogs? Is parking covered? How long is the drive downtown at 8 AM?

More of those questions now go to Google or an AI assistant before anyone calls the office. If the answer isn't written down somewhere they can find it, the renter usually moves on to a community where it is.

The brochure still matters. The answers matter more.

Now look for each answer on the site, in plain words, on a page that loads without clicking through three menus.

If you had to hunt for it, an AI assistant probably won't find it either. And when an assistant can't find an answer, it tends to recommend a community where it can.

posts.text:
Renters check the date on your photos.
Maybe not on purpose, but they notice.

A pool shot taken in summer, a holiday wreath in April, a model unit with furniture the office replaced two years ago. None of it is wrong. It just quietly tells a renter nobody is paying attention.

Fresh photos are one of the easiest signals to control:

• Add a few new ones every month, in the season you're in
• Retire anything that no longer matches what a renter will see on a tour
• Keep the same photos on Google, the website and the listing sites

posts.alt: Rooftop pool with palm trees and a city view

posts.text:
Posting more is not a strategy.
Posting what renters ask about is.

Seven posts a week of "Happy Monday" and stock sunsets will fill a calendar. It rarely fills a tour schedule.

The posts that pull their weight answer something: what is included, what the neighborhood is like, which homes are available, what the team is like to work with. They match the website and the Google listing, and they change with the season.

Frequency still matters. It just comes second.
